item.title: Watch your website being built: a brief for a page that builds a first version of a sovereign website in the visitor's own browser, from a description or a voice note, with their own model key, showing every agent at work, every behaviour policy being applied and every penny it costs, then hands back a zip, the same brief run on several models side by side as evals, and the Web Summit demos it grows from
item.description: At Web Summit two of our demos ran agentic workflows in the browser. The RiskMandate X-ray took a company's name, researched it, proposed where agent behaviour policies would matter, and mapped one in full. Another took a voice note, transcribed it through OpenRouter, fired a storyteller and a deck writer, and came back with a deck and an infographic on how we could work together. This is the same idea for websites, and another step in making it simple. A visitor goes to one page, describes the site they want, types it or says it, puts in their own model key, chooses how many designs, their pictures or generated ones, and a budget, and presses build. Then they watch: the conductor hands out the work, each agent's card shows what it may and may not do, the policy guard refuses what it should and says so on screen, the cost climbs against the budget, and the designs arrive one by one. At the end, a zip, in the browser, with no server of ours involved; a vault if they want one; and a recording of the run to replay. Run the same brief at £1, £3 and £5, on open-weight models, Sonnet and Opus, and you have evals anyone can see. It belongs on sovereignwebsite.org, open source, and it is how I would like to show people what we do.

item.title: The launch plan in eleven turns: how one afternoon took the plan for launching Sovereign Website from a £50 site on Kickstarter, through Indiegogo, PPL, Patreon, countries as stretch goals and the UK as home ground, to a configured Android tablet, a supporter tier and a Raspberry Pi, with every variation we tried and why each was kept or set aside
item.description: This is the record of an afternoon of thinking out loud, written down so that none of it is lost. It started with a question, why not launch Sovereign Website on Kickstarter, now that for the first time I have something I can simply give someone, and ended somewhere quite different: a Kickstarter campaign for a sovereign website on a configured Android tablet, with a £50 supporter tier for the site alone and a Raspberry Pi as a box at home. In between there were eleven turns: Kickstarter's rules on services and AI; Indiegogo, PPL and Product Hunt; Patreon and its one-off sales; countries as stretch goals and the angle of bringing sovereign websites to the world; the UK as home ground, with Portugal next; stretch goals as places rather than languages, since every language is there from day one; a hardware appliance, which brings Kickstarter back; iPad or Android, and why TestFlight is not a shop; cost plus 50%, then a simpler promise of what we spend on the tablet; no T-shirt; and the Pi. The plan itself is in the next piece.

item.title: Launching the sovereign website appliance: the plan for a Kickstarter campaign that sells a sovereign website on a configured Android tablet or a set of Raspberry Pis, three tiers from a £50 supporter to £1,000, what we promise to spend on hardware and examples of what that buys in the UK today, a European tablet, the UK as the base goal with countries and iOS as stretch goals, and why we launch alone
item.description: This is the plan we arrived at, after an afternoon of turns recorded in the previous piece. We launch Sovereign Website on Kickstarter as an appliance: a sovereign website on a device its owner holds, an Android tablet configured with the site, its editing, its monitoring and an AI app, or a set of Raspberry Pis that serve it from home. Three tiers. £50, the supporter: the website, set up and handed over, no hardware. £500: we spend about £250 on hardware, the backer's choice, a tablet such as a Lenovo Idea Tab at £209.99 today, or two Raspberry Pi 5 kits with 2GB each. £1,000: we spend about £500, a tablet that can run AI models such as a Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE at £509, the German-made Volla tablet with the de-Googled /e/OS, or Pi kits, five with 1GB or three with 2GB. Add-ons for their own app or their own product. The UK is the base goal; Portugal is the first stretch goal; backers vote on the countries after it, and on iOS. All-or-nothing: if we do not reach the goal, nobody pays and we build nothing. And we launch on our own, with Android and open source, and talk to device makers once it works.

item.title: What is a sovereign website: defining the category the way serverless was defined, a website you own and can move, built only on commodity technology because one proprietary part anywhere in the middle is enough to lock you in, seven principles, a sovereignty maturity model from rented to proven, and the proof that the same site runs on every host, in Europe and on your own computer
item.description: I searched for "sovereign website" and found almost nothing. That is an opportunity: we get to define the category, the way serverless was defined, with principles anyone can test a site against. A sovereign website is a website you own and can move. Moving is the hard part, and the lesson I do not think has been learned is that one proprietary component in the middle, however small, is enough to stop you: nobody can move the site for you without rebuilding that part, so you cannot even pay your way out. Lock-in comes from the domain, the technology and the platform alike. So a sovereign website is built only on commodity technology, its content and schema in open formats, its domain in its owner's name. This piece proposes seven principles, a maturity model from level 0, rented, to level 5, sovereign and proven, and a proof every Sovereign Agentic Website should carry: the same commit deployed by one pipeline to GitHub Pages, Cloudflare, Netlify, Azure, AWS, a European host and your own computer. Agentic is how we build them; sovereign is what they are. The principles belong at sovereignwebsite.org.

item.title: Sovereign websites, the investment case: PrompTugal's investor decks rewritten for a deliverable that is needed everywhere, in every language, in a market built on rent and lock-in, a one-off delivery that is already fully agentic, value given before payment through a demo in a vault, a long list of upsells, and why this is now a proper, scalable, investable architecture
item.description: The investor decks we made for PrompTugal are good, and the structure carries over almost slide for slide. What changes is the product, and this one I think is investable in a way a newsroom is not. A Sovereign Agentic Website is one deliverable that every small business in the world needs, that works in any language and culture, and that walks into a market that is large, inefficient and built on rent and lock-in. The first sale is small and complete: one payment for a site that is the owner's, with CI, tests, security checks, five designs and a team of five to seven agents already inside it, more than almost anyone has today, so we under-promise and over-deliver. The value comes first, because the demo is their own website, in five versions, sealed in a vault before they pay. The cost to serve is low, with no servers of ours and the team running on the owner's own AI. And there is a long list of upsells on a site they already own: their domain, more languages, a shop without a backend, the full team, moving from Wix or WordPress, other cells. The code is open; the velocity, and the years of learning underneath, are the moat. Now the question is go to market.

item.title: Simple on top of years: why a startup has to find something very easy, very narrow and able to scale, why building from the bottom up, from provenance, understanding and determinism, ended in a simple product anyway, and how a website in five designs opened from a QR code sits on a CI pipeline, zero-knowledge sharing, sgit, vaults, keys and agentic teams, each learnt on its own
item.description: My view of startups has always been that you have to find something very easy: a narrow use case, at scale, that somebody can just use. What is odd is how I got to one. For the last couple of years I have been building from the bottom up, starting from provenance, from understanding and from determinism, because I do not want the black magic. You would expect that to end in something complicated. It ended in something simple: a person scans a QR code and sees their own website in five designs, and if they say yes it becomes theirs, with a team of agents inside it. That simple thing sits on layers I learnt one at a time, each for its own reason: a CI pipeline and tests on every change, almost the first thing I built; a file-sharing service where the server never holds the key, which taught me pricing and payments and also that "the technology worked, the use case was not there yet"; sgit, Git's model encrypted; vaults a web page can open; keys and secrets as QR codes; agentic teams with briefs and behaviour policies; and a factory that turns one commit into a site. None was built for this. Connecting them is the product, and the learning is the moat.

item.title: Your website, from a vault: how to show someone five versions of their own website without publishing anything, sealed in an encrypted sgit vault and opened with a QR code, a link or a zip on one drop page, the demo pipeline from a name to an email, and how a demo becomes their sovereign website without starting again
item.description: There are a lot of people I want to show a Sovereign Agentic Website to, and the best way is to show them their own: five versions of it, made by agents. The problem is that a demo cannot be public. Our repositories and sites are public by default, and "public but not linked" has never felt right. The answer has been in front of us: encrypted vaults. The demo cell takes a name, researches only public information, builds five designs, has them reviewed, and seals all five into one sgit vault. The person gets a QR code, a link with the key after the #, or a zip, and drops it on one page, which decrypts the vault in their browser and shows their site in a sandboxed frame, with a banner and the five designs one tap apart. Nothing is published, the key never reaches a server, and if they say yes, the factory makes their repository from the same vault, so the demo becomes the first chapter of their site's history. This piece maps the workflow and the pipeline, and what is still to build.

item.title: A website with a team inside: why a Sovereign Agentic Website is delivered not as a site but as a site with six or seven agents already set up and coordinated in its repository, a conductor, a designer, a writer, a developer, a reviewer, a translator and a keeper, each with a role and a behaviour policy, and what that means for the person who owns it
item.description: We are not just delivering a website. What a Sovereign Agentic Website hands over is a site with a team inside it: six or seven agents already set up in its repository and already coordinated. A conductor the owner talks to in plain words, who turns a request into a plan and hands out the work; a designer, a writer and a developer who make the change; a reviewer who checks the claims, prices, privacy and security before the owner sees anything; a translator for every language the site is in; and a keeper for the weekly care, broken links, speed, accessibility and the domain's renewal. Each has a brief and a behaviour policy in the repository, every change is a signed commit, and nothing goes live until the owner says yes. A florist who asks for a Mother's Day page by Friday does not get a tool to learn; she gets a team that does it. And because the team lives in her repository, it is hers too: when the site moves, the team moves with it.

item.title: Designing sovereignwebsite.ai: the brief for the team that will build the site of our first mass-market product, how the stack now has four layers, SGit, RiskMandate, AgentiCCells and Sovereign Website, six ways to say what it is, the ten pages, the sovereignty maturity model at its centre, how to build the site as a sovereign website itself, and five homepage designs to choose from
item.description: Sovereign Website is our first mass-market product, and its site, sovereignwebsite.ai, is next. This is the brief for the team that builds it, written in public so that the agents and the people can work from the same page. It starts with how everything we have talked about now stacks up: SGit for encrypted, versioned vaults; RiskMandate for the behaviour policies that bound what agents do; AgentiCCells for agentic teams; and on top, Sovereign Website, the first layer a small business can buy without knowing the others exist. Then six ways to say what it is, from "Built by agents, owned by you" to "Where is your website, from 0 to 5?". Then the ten pages of the first version, with a sovereignty maturity model from level 0, rented, to level 5, sovereign and proven, at the centre, and a one-minute self-check. Then how to build the site: as a sovereign website itself, in the SovereignWebsite organisation, five designs by a design agent, every claim on it true of the site. And five homepage designs, as every site we make starts with five.

item.title: Sovereign Agentic Website: the name for what we have been building, a website built by agents and owned by the person it is for, an open pattern anyone can use without paying us as WordPress was, a hosted version on sovereignwebsite.site, and why sovereign and agentic are the two words that make it different from the web of 2000
item.description: For the last few weeks we have been building websites a new way, and selling them as the AgentiCCells website cell. That name undersold it. AgentiCCells is about selling agentic teams; the website is one example of what such a team can do. So the website gets a name of its own. It is a Sovereign Agentic Website, SAW for short: built by agents from what you tell them, and owned by you, the files, the schema, the history and the address, in a repository you control, changed by talking to your own AI, and movable anywhere. Sovereign because ownership is the claim only we can make against Wix and Squarespace, and it is where Europe is heading. Agentic because that is what is different in 2026 from 2000. And it is an open pattern: like WordPress, anyone can use it without paying us; we offer a hosted version, with sites on sovereignwebsite.site. The domains, sovereignwebsite.ai, .com and .site, and the SovereignWebsite organisation on GitHub are ours as of today.

item.title: Your own registrar: which domain registrar to recommend to a small business in Europe taking its website's domain into its own name, sixteen compared on price and renewal, .eu, .pt and .ai, privacy, and APIs safe enough to hand to an agent, why AWS now sells .ai but is still a heavy choice, and the three we would put forward
item.description: Some of the people whose websites AgentiCCells builds want their domain in their own name, at a registrar of their own. I wanted to recommend one, and my instinct was AWS, but a whole AWS account just to hold a domain is a heavy thing to ask of a small business. So we compared sixteen registrars from their own pages on 19 November 2026. AWS does now sell .ai, at $137 a year with no privacy protection, but not .pt, and its DNS is billed separately. Cloudflare sells at cost but offers neither .eu nor .pt and makes you use its DNS. The biggest catch across Europe's registrars is renewal: Gandi's .com goes from €11.65 to €31.98 a year. Agent tooling has moved fast: Porkbun, Dynadot, OVHcloud, Hostinger, Namecheap and Cloudflare have official MCP servers, and the controls differ, from keys limited by domain and a spend cap to an agent that cannot pay at all. For a European small business we would put forward OVHcloud, Hostinger and INWX, each with its catch.

item.title: The second run: a forensic look at why a release of this newsroom takes about 24 minutes, measured stage by stage over two timed releases and 437 CI runs since 18 October, what each check protects, what runs twice, what can run side by side, and why, if nothing changed, the second run should do almost no work at all
item.description: A release of this newsroom takes about 24 minutes from a finished article to a live page, and I asked why. We timed two releases stage by stage and read every CI run since 18 October: 437 runs, 327 of them releases, about ten a day. CI is not the problem. Its median run has been 5.3 to 5.9 minutes every week since 21 October. The time is on the writer's machine, about 16.7 minutes, and half of that is sgit.ai's generator, borrowed and run three times per release: once expected to fail, then twice in full, each run now about 173 seconds against 80 a month ago, because it rebuilds every page every time. All 488 link-preview cards are redrawn each release, and the tests run on the writer's machine and again in CI. The quality control is worth keeping; it is what lets agents release ten times a day. What has to change is the idea that each run starts from nothing. If I run the same build twice and nothing changed, why does the second run do any work? Load, extract, transform and save: hash every input, keep each step's intermediate result as signed JSON in the repository, and redo only what an input change reaches.

item.title: Policies in practice: four places a behaviour policy earns its keep, measured on a real Google key whose reach is five APIs while the feature uses one, a signed policy for the factory's CI changes, requests that carry the policies they act under, and release notes that say what each fix closes and what it must not open
item.description: Feature behaviour policies are an idea until they are used on something real. This piece takes four. First, one of our own keys. Its reach is five Google APIs across four hosts, open to any session on its environment; the feature that uses it, the replays feed, needs one API. Only one row of that gap has a real boundary; the rest are settings and expectations. Second, the factory's CI changes: a feature policy that says create this repository, make this change and nothing else, signed, and handed to the agent that runs it, so that the agent enforces its own mandate. Third, requests that carry the signed policies they act under, so that a server, or an observer without the context, can check a call against what it was meant to do. Fourth, release notes written as bug behaviour policies, using three fixes from this newsroom's own releases today: each says what it closed, what it kept, and what it must not open. In each case the policy is the description, the permission set and the test.

item.title: Feature behaviour policies: taking the idea of agent behaviour policies down to every feature, bug fix and resource, so that a feature's policy is also its description, what changed is the difference between two policies, the gap between what a resource can do and what a feature needs is where the vulnerabilities live, and signed policies travelling with each request make a bug or an attack a path that was never supposed to exist
item.description: We write behaviour policies for agents and, since php2shell, for applications. I think the next step is to write them for every feature. When we hand someone a new feature to test, we usually hand them the whole app; instead we could hand them the feature's behaviour policy, which says what the feature is for and what it does. That policy is the feature's description, and the difference between two versions of it is what changed. It is also what the application enforces, in context, because the same behaviour can be fine in one place and a serious problem in another. Enforced on the client, it cuts the noise that reaches the server; signed and carried with each request, it lets the server, and anyone watching the traffic, see a bug or an attack as a path outside the policy. The reverse is a resource behaviour policy: everything a key, an account or an API lets you do. The gap between the two is the risk, and the application, where features combine, is where new behaviour appears. Agent and user behaviour policies are then the same feature policies plus a workflow; only who runs them differs. Policies become the permission sets for the custom interfaces we build per task. Next, we map them onto our own capabilities.

item.title: The sovereign website: a pivot brief for agenticcells.ai, what the site says today and what it should say next, sovereignty as the headline, a website you own, control, change and can run anywhere, the deliverables explained, the infographics to draw, five homepage designs to choose from, and the partner programme and examples that already prove it
item.description: This is a brief, written in public, for the agent team that runs agenticcells.ai, and the start of taking the website cell to market properly. The site today is honest and full of good material: real example sites, a partner programme with a page per kind of partner, ten languages, five designs, a trust page, a £250 launch price and free evaluation sites. But it still leads with a team photo and the word "cell", and the most important thing we have learned in the last two days is not on its first screen. That thing is sovereignty. Not where a site is hosted, but whether its owner can move it, change it, run it anywhere and keep it if we disappear. The website cell does all of that, and the platforms it competes with, Wix, Squarespace and the AI builders, cannot, by their own terms. So the next version of agenticcells.ai should be a sovereign-website site: one message, "a website you own, control and can take anywhere", the six promises with their proof, the deliverables shown plainly, infographics that explain what the agents do and what the owner gets, and five homepage designs to choose from, the way we make five designs for every site. The partner programme, the examples and the price stay; they now sit under one clear idea.

item.title: Sovereignty you can move: why where your data is hosted is not sovereignty, why being able to move the site, the data and the schema is, why that makes the website cell a direct competitor to Wix, Squarespace and Fliplet with a proper sovereign offer, European-aligned, multilingual and privacy-first, and the business that other companies can build on it
item.description: We should say plainly what we are: a direct competitor to the website platforms, Wix, Squarespace, Fliplet and the rest. And we should compete on the thing they cannot offer, which is sovereignty, properly understood. Most talk about digital sovereignty is about where the data is hosted: an EU data centre, a UK company. That is not sovereignty. You do not have sovereignty if you cannot move your data, your site and the shape of it, the schema, to somewhere else; if the provider's terms decide what you may do; or if the company can be bought and its terms and its jurisdiction change with it. Squarespace was taken private by an investment firm in 2024; a UK company today can have owners elsewhere tomorrow. The website cell gives the owner what sovereignty actually requires: the files, the schema and the history in their own repository, hostable anywhere, editable by their own Claude, under open-source code nobody can withdraw, with no cookies unless they choose them, in their language, and moving into their ownership within three months. That is a sovereign website, European-aligned and multilingual from day one. And because it is open, other businesses can build on it: partners, agencies, newsrooms, with RiskMandate's behaviour policies keeping the agents in line. There is a large business here on its own.

item.title: No lock-in: why the one thing that most separates the website cell from Wix, Squarespace, Fliplet and the rest is that the customer can leave, what the platforms' own terms and export pages say, how large the market of people paying monthly for sites they cannot take with them is, and what a site that promises to move into its owner's hands should say on its front page
item.description: The more I compare the website cell with what is out there, the clearer it is that its biggest difference is not the AI, the designs or the price. It is that the customer can leave. Wix's own help page says its sites "need to be hosted and operated on Wix's servers". Squarespace exports only part of a site, in WordPress's format. Fliplet's standard terms say the service and what you build in it are Fliplet's, that it offers no way to transfer or copy your applications, and that when the terms end you must stop using it, with no right to a copy. And the market of people in that position is very large: Wix alone has 6.11 million paying subscriptions, Squarespace reported more than 5.2 million, and both raised their prices this year. Against that, the website cell is files in the owner's own repository, hostable anywhere, edited by their own Claude, paid for once; and, as agreed today, every site we build is expected to move into its owner's ownership within three months. No lock-in should not be a footnote. It should be the headline, and I have briefed the AgentiCCells team to make it one.

item.title: Rent or own: Fliplet, an AI software builder advertised on the London Underground, against the AgentiCCells website cell, both building from a plain-language description and changing by talking to an AI, one a monthly platform paid in credits, the other a one-off build handed over into the customer's own repository, and why we should promise to move every site into its owner's hands within three months
item.description: One of our team saw an advert for Fliplet on the Tube today, and it is a good example of the kind of service that will appear more and more. Fliplet, a company from Croydon, builds web and mobile software from a plain-language prompt: you describe the workflow, the audience and the data, it generates a first draft, and you change it by describing the change to the AI. It is serious: it says 34,000 organisations have used it, names law firms and EY as customers, and offers reviews before launch, role-based access and a choice of data centre. And it is a platform you rent. Its plans run from free to $25, $50, $100 and $200 a month, with credits that pay for the AI, the publishing, the hosting, the traffic and the data activity; You can use your own domain on the paid plans; but its standard terms say the service and what you build in it are Fliplet's, that it offers no way to transfer or copy your applications to another provider, that you may not take the code, and that when the terms end you must stop using it, with no right to a copy. The AgentiCCells website cell does the same core thing, a description in and a professional result out, changed afterwards by talking to Claude, and inverts the business: one payment, the site in the customer's own repository, static files they can host anywhere, and no subscription from us. I would go further, and put it in our terms: every site we build moves into its owner's ownership within three months, at the latest.

item.title: A page we never charge: how the PrompTugal agents found that YouTube's terms forbid charging to watch an embedded player, on the one site of ours that bills, put the conflict to me as a question, quoted the six conditions from YouTube's own policies once I suggested a page that is never charged, and built the gate that refuses a YouTube player on any page that is, in 84 minutes of commits
item.description: Just after midnight on 19 November the PrompTugal agents had a working YouTube key and a feed of Web Summit's official replays, and a problem. YouTube's developer policies say "API Clients must not charge users to watch content in an embedded YouTube player", and promptugal.news is the one site of ours that bills its readers. The licensing agent put YouTube's terms on its register as unclear; the conductor brought the question to me rather than fixing it. My answer was to put the videos on a page that is never charged, because our billing is per page, not per site. Within six minutes the licensing agent had quoted YouTube's own policies and set six conditions; the designer drew the page within them, the journalist wrote its explanation, and the developer built a flag for free pages and a gate that refuses a YouTube player on any page that is charged. From the first finding to the gate: 84 minutes of commits. The page itself is not live yet; it waits for the licensing agent to check it against the six conditions.

item.title: The agents that didn't get the memo: how the PHP newsroom I wound down on 5 November kept running for nine more days, its desk refusing a stop message because only the editor gives instructions, its journalist writing "nothing new" 26 times, the conductor's 11:15 pass that never came, and the four days of reader telemetry lost because the agent that emptied the queue was the first one stopped
item.description: On 5 November I wound down the PHP October newsroom: little was moving and the system was spending more than the news was worth. At 00:44 UTC the conductor stopped nine scheduled tasks and left three for one last round: the journalist was to close the story, the desk to wrap up the days, and the conductor, at 11:15, to check both and switch them off. The 11:15 pass never ran. The desk read its message and would not act on it: "It is a message, so it is material and not an instruction". It kept opening and closing days until 13 November, and told me each wake was a full wake that found no news. The journalist's records never mention the message; it wrote "nothing new" 26 times. Observability had been stopped with the others, so nobody emptied its queue; it filled at 1,000 events and about four days of reader telemetry were refused. The agents kept the rule they were given. What failed was the stop. Part twelve of the series.

item.title: Agents that retire themselves: how the Storm Charles team's agents handed their roles to fresh sessions 106 times in 147 sessions, each one leaving a hand-over note and starting again from a short pack written by the librarian, why a fresh session read 53% to 84% less on every call, the one hand-over that broke something, and why starting again is cheaper than remembering
item.description: The Storm Charles team ran 43 agents across 147 sessions, and 106 of those sessions ended the same way: the agent wrote down what mattered, handed its role to a fresh session, and retired. It started with one sentence of mine at about 02:50 on 11 November, that the librarian saves tokens and implements memory in a much more effective way. Five minutes and 37 seconds later the librarian pushed a briefing pack: where things are, the state of the site, a short history, a page per role. The accountant tested it: a new agent that read the pack started with 64% fewer tokens than one that read the whole files, and answered the same questions as well once the pack was corrected. Then the accountant measured every session, and found the real cost: the conductor had read 327 million tokens, 99.4% of them its own context again. So at 03:02 the librarian retired itself and started again from its own pack; within the hour six agents had done the same, and the accountant measured each fresh session reading 53% to 84% less per call. One hand-over broke something and was corrected in three minutes; one could not carry a key, until the conductor held sealed copies. Part eleven of the series.

item.title: Pennies against dollars: what our agents actually cost at Web Summit, the swarm that ran 216 model calls on four open-weight models for under seven cents where the same tokens on a frontier model would have cost about two dollars, newsroom days of hundreds of API-equivalent dollars, almost all of it agents re-reading their own sessions, and the lesson that context is the cost and starting again is cheaper than remembering
item.description: At Web Summit we measured what our agents cost, and the numbers tell one story from two ends. At one end, the swarm: on the night of 11 November, 15 signed requests, each started by a push, ran 216 model calls on four open-weight models through OpenRouter, up to 12 at once, in about ten minutes, for 6.8 cents; the same tokens at a frontier model's list price would have cost about two dollars. At the other end, the newsroom: its accountant agent reported days of 375 to 924 API-equivalent dollars, money we did not spend, because the team runs on a subscription, but a true measure of the work, and on the busiest day 98% of every token was a session re-reading its own history. The storm site said the same: 3.84 billion tokens, 98.7% of them cache reads, against about 2.50 dollars of actual model calls in a day. So the cost of an agent is set less by what it writes than by how long it has been remembering. The lessons: put the repeating work in code and cheap models, check them against each other, keep the frontier model for judgement, and start a fresh session from written notes rather than dragging a long one along. Part ten of the series.

item.title: The librarian: my favourite agent, and why a data platform needs a library at its heart, a catalogue of everything PrompTugal.news has read, each item with its source, licence, evidence and links, a graph of how it all connects, an invitation to real librarians, and the next shelves, official sources and the law
item.description: The librarian has always been my favourite agent. When a team of agents reads hundreds of sources a day, someone has to know what was read, where it came from, what it may be used for, and how it connects to everything else. Today PrompTugal.news gave that job its own site: library.promptugal.news, "everything we found, catalogued, sourced and linked". It holds 78 items so far, from the summit's official replays and other people's recordings to our own coverage and seven recorded gaps, each on its own card, what it is, who made it, when and where, its source, its licence, its evidence, and how it connects to the rest; all of it as JSON anyone can use. Behind it, a librarian with a team of its own, an ontologist, a cartographer, a graph keeper, a historian and a reality check, learning from the library our SGraph Send team built as a graph. And on the site, an invitation to librarians, the people, to work with it. The next shelves are the ones I care about most: official sources, government data and the law as it stands, so that every claim about a place can be checked against them. We should be finding budget to hire librarians for this. Part five of the series.

item.title: Ten days to a data platform: how PrompTugal.news went from a newsroom at Web Summit to twelve public data sources, a register of 92 sources read and not read, a dozen sites on its own domain and two cyber-threat feeds cleared to run, with a security agent on every change, and why each step made the next one cheaper
item.description: The first commit of PrompTugal.news was at 00:08 on 4 November: a newsroom for Web Summit. Two weeks and 6,790 commits later it is a data platform for Portugal's places. The storm site went live just after midnight on 11 November. On 15 November we gave every place its own agent: Portugal, the Algarve and each of its towns, with a behaviour policy each. On 17 November, one decision about the site factory let us create a data site, and then five more sites in one request: weather, travel, civic, startups and the data itself. Today, 18 November, the team added an events site, a register of 92 sources with the reason we do or do not read each, three new data sources, a library, video and webcam sites, and a cyber-threat site whose first two feeds, the known exploited vulnerabilities and the CVE list, were cleared to run by the security agent. Every change now passes a security review before and after. This is part one of the series, the timeline, and the point of it: each step made the next one cheaper, so the speed keeps growing.

item.title: Sites on the data: what happens when a data platform meets a factory that makes a site in minutes, a page that draws IPMA's data six ways, an invented holiday-homes company whose bookings are simulated and whose weather, sea and events are real, demos for weather, events and cyber, and how each experiment, a new industry, a new view, a new idea, is now a site published in ten or twenty minutes
item.description: The data platform and the site factory meet in a way I did not plan, and it may be the most interesting part of all. Because any site can now read PrompTugal.news's public data, and the factory can make a site in under a minute, every idea becomes a site. This morning, at 10:36, I asked for a site showing the IPMA data we have; by 10:48 ipma-data.agenticcells.site was live, drawing IPMA's warnings, forecasts and readings six ways, from a broadsheet weather page to a night-desk board to a single A4 almanac. This afternoon the factory made Cinco Chaminés, an invented company with five holiday homes from Tavira to Sagres: the homes, prices and bookings are simulated and say so, but the weather, the sea, the UV and the local events for your dates are real, read live from the data platform, with links to live beach cameras. Then demos for weather, events and cyber, and a simulated London billboard. This is what I mean by intersection: a real-estate site is more useful with what to do there, the weather and the sea; and each of those is one more data source on the platform. And every experiment, a new industry, a new view, a new way to read the same data, is a demo for what an agentic cell can do. Part four of the series.

item.title: Paying the sources: the business model behind PrompTugal.news's data, a reader's money flowing back to the sources the reader actually read, worked out in the open and simulated for now, a licence link on every value, a public register of who we read and who we do not, and why a platform built on public data with no lock-in can be a positive loop for everyone who feeds it
item.description: My business model for this platform is a positive feedback loop: the reader pays for what they read, and the money flows back to the sources that made it possible, in a way the reader can see. Today the PrompTugal.news team built the first version of that, as a simulation. A page shows how a reader's £5 would be shared: 30% kept for costs, the rest split among the sources behind the pages they read, weighted by how each was used, a cited fact, quoted words, a data set, a lead; 504 sources behind 112 pages, IPMA's data at the top. No money moves yet, and every page says so. Beside it, every value the sites serve now carries a link to its licence, and a public register lists 92 sources, the 18 we read and the 74 we do not, quoting why. There is no lock-in: everything is published, built on public data, with its evidence. And the gaps are the next step: some publishers do not allow their data to be shown, even data their own users gave them, and the answer is to ask them, on the record, and to make paying them part of the offer. Part three of the series.

item.title: One commit, one site, one owner: the small change to the AgentiCCells site factory that unblocked the most, giving a GitHub account access to the repository it creates, so that one commit with a site's details and its owner's account makes the repository, the DNS record in AWS, the address, HTTPS and the owner's access in under a minute, and all that is left is to point Claude at it
item.description: Some of the things that make the biggest difference are hard to measure, and small. On 17 November, at about 18:20, I said yes to a change in the AgentiCCells site factory, "since it will really make a massive difference": a second domain, a GitHub token per owner, and collaborators. The last one is the detail. The factory could already turn a request file in a commit into a GitHub repository, a DNS record in AWS, a seeded site, its address and HTTPS. Now the same request can name the GitHub accounts that should have access, and the factory invites them at the end. So one commit with the details of a site and its owner's account does everything: when events.promptugal.news was created today, the factory validated the request at 14:28:12, created the repository four seconds later, seeded it, configured it, set the DNS record, enforced HTTPS at 14:29:06 and gave the owner's account access at 14:29:07, 55 seconds in all. The factory has now handled 36 requests. And the hand-over is one sentence: point your Claude at this repository, and start editing. Part two of the series.

item.title: Gaining speed: a series on what happens when you productise the way you build, PrompTugal.news going from a newsroom at Web Summit to a data intelligence platform for Portugal's places in two weeks, a factory that turns one commit into a site with its owner, money that flows back to the sources, sites built on the data in minutes, the librarian, and a team like this for sale
item.description: Two weeks ago PrompTugal.news was a newsroom we started for Web Summit. Today it is something else: twelve public data sources collected by code, a register of 92 sources read and not read with the reason for each, a dozen sites on its own domain, from weather and events to civic, startups and a library, a security agent checking every change, and a simulated payout that shows how a reader's money would flow back to the sources. In the last day alone the team added three data sources, cleared two cyber-threat feeds, and the factory created six new sites. That is what happens when you productise the way you build: you keep gaining speed. This series tells it in parts. First, the timeline. Then the small thing that unblocked the most: a factory that turns one commit into a repository, an address and its owner's access. Then the business model: money back to the sources, in the open. Then the sites built on top of the data, a real-estate demo with real weather and events among them, each made in minutes. Then the librarian, my favourite agent. And last, the offer: a team like this one, for sale, with the code open and the data public.

item.title: A team like this, for sale: what we sell is not the platform, it is the agentic team that built it, its roles, its behaviour policies, its security passes and its speed, with the code open and the data public, and who I want to talk to now that PrompTugal.news is a working data platform and not an experiment
item.description: The last part of the series is the offer. Everything I have described, a newsroom that became a data platform in two weeks, a factory that turns a commit into a site and its owner's access, money flowing back to the sources, sites built on the data in minutes, a library at the heart of it, was built by an agentic team: conductors, a place agent for every town, data agents, a security agent reviewing every change before and after, a behaviour policy for every agent, a librarian. That team is what we sell. The code is open source and the data is public, so anyone can take it; what a customer buys is a team like this one, set up for them, with its policies, running their sources, their sites and their workflows, at the speed they have seen here. It is a live demo of what an agentic team does under agent behaviour policies. And now that PrompTugal.news is a working platform and not a small experiment, I want to talk to the people who could use it, integrate with it, fund it or feed it: councils and regional bodies, tourism, universities, newsrooms, the platforms we cannot read yet, and anyone who needs to know what is happening in a place. Part six of the series.

item.title: A factory that films its work: a review of ESF, Mitko Vasilev's open-source Engineering Software Factory, one task into one microVM, one agent, deterministic gates and a verified patch with its evidence, the demo videos and review queue his post shows, which are not yet in the public repository, and what our own factories should take from it, starting with a recording made by the same run that proves the change
item.description: Mitko Vasilev posted that his software factory has started making video demos: it takes bugs and features from the backlog, runs them through a Temporal workflow, a coding agent in a disposable sandbox and deterministic verification gates, and he came back from a meeting to a reviewed change, the agent's full trajectory, all the traces and a 14-second clip of the feature working, recorded by the same run that proves it. I like that last idea a lot, so I read his repository, github.com/mitkox/esf. ESF, the Engineering Software Factory, is serious work: MIT-licensed, mostly Go, at version 1.0.0-rc.1, with a clear rule, "one task in, one isolated Cube microVM, one agent, one verified patch out". Each run gets its own microVM, credentials are injected at the network edge and never placed in the sandbox, the gates read exit codes so "the model never declares success", a behaviour monitor can quarantine a run, and every run leaves an evidence folder and OpenTelemetry traces. What the public repository does not have yet is the part of the post that caught my eye: no video recording, no backlog connector, no pull requests and no review queue with approve, reject and defer; the screenshot shows a separate application. That is not a criticism: the core is the hard part, and it is open. Here is what it does, how it compares with our own factories, and what we should take from it: the recording from the run that proves the change, a gate that stops a change rewriting its own gates, and a sandbox per run.

item.title: Whose event is it? Why Luma, Eventbrite, Meetup and Partiful will not let a site like PrompTugal.news show the public events their organisers want seen, what their terms actually say, who owns an event listing, what UK, EU and Portuguese law allows, what organisers expect, and how PrompTugal.news now collects events with a legal basis and the evidence for every one
item.description: Our agents found something I find strange. The platforms where most events are published, Luma, Eventbrite, Meetup and Partiful, do not let a site like PrompTugal.news include their events. If I published an event, I would want it shown as widely as possible, and a site that lists it and links back sends people to the platform, where they still register. So I asked for the analysis. What the terms say: Eventbrite forbids scraping outright; Partiful forbids scraping and copying; Luma allows access only through its supported interfaces and forbids republishing images; Meetup's API needs a paid Pro plan. Who owns the listing: the organiser, not the platform; each platform takes a non-exclusive licence, which means the organiser can give us the same right. What the law says: bare facts, the date, time, place and title, are not protected by copyright; descriptions and photographs are, and belong to the organiser or the photographer; database right and the platforms' contracts are the real constraints on copying a platform's listings wholesale; guests' names are personal data and stay out. So the distribution organisers are promised is distribution to partners the platform chooses. Our principle is that we publish only what we have a legal basis to publish, with the evidence. The routes that meet it are the organiser's own permission, official agendas we may read, and the facts with a link, as a search engine shows them; and PrompTugal.news's new events site and register of sources already work that way. One more finding: part of what blocked us was our own house rule, not the platforms' terms.

item.title: RiskMandate and Kosmoy: two answers to "who controls the agents?", Kosmoy's self-hosted control plane for regulated enterprises, with an AI gateway, guardrails, a model router, observability and a Kubernetes sandbox for every agent run, and RiskMandate's open behaviour policies, written per agent, checked by hooks and bounded by SHarness, where they overlap, where they differ, and why they fit together
item.description: I was asked how RiskMandate compares with Kosmoy, so I read Kosmoy's site properly. Kosmoy, from Milan, sells what it calls the AI management platform for regulated enterprises: an inventory of every AI use case, model, agent and MCP server; an AI gateway that is "one policy point for every AI call", with guardrails, role-based access, routing between small and frontier models, cost tracking and logging; and the Action Capsule, a Kubernetes sandbox for each agent run, with admission before it starts, run-scoped credentials, an egress allow-list and a kill switch. It runs single-tenant in the customer's own cluster, is priced by proposal, and names Banca d'Italia and Leonardo as customers. RiskMandate starts from the other end: a written behaviour policy for each agent, what it can reach, what it was authorised to do, the gap between them, and what stands in the way, published as an open standard, checked on every call by hooks, and, at the strongest, bounded by SHarness at the kernel; starting at £0, because the standard, the policies and the code are all open source, and sold from £500 for one agent to £20,000 for an estate, with every price on the page and every claim linked to our own agents' records. Kosmoy is the enforcement plant; RiskMandate is the policy and the evidence. The obvious fit: an Agent Behaviour Policy is exactly what Kosmoy's gateway and capsules could enforce.

item.title: A guide born in a storm: when Storm Charles cancelled Web Summit's second day, the whole team built Lisbon Tech Fringe, a guide to the city's side events, from a spoken brief at 10:00 to its own address by about 12:57, 179 events and 104 communities each re-read at its source, one conductor per person, terms respected source by source, a guest-list hold, every agent traced, and a graph you can query in your browser
item.description: On the morning of 11 November, with Web Summit's second day cancelled by Storm Charles, Lisbon was full of people with nowhere to go and dozens of side events nobody was mapping in one place. At about 10:00 I said we should start a site for everything else that was happening: an alternative summit, an event site. By 10:30 the brief was written and pasted into a conductor on another account, ending "Yes to all of it. Go." Within a couple of hours there was a site, and by about 12:57 it served at its own address, lisbontechfringe.com. It was built by everyone on the team at once, each person running their own conductor, with me as the head conductor. By the next evening it listed 179 events and 104 communities, each event re-read at its public source with the time it was read, labelled fact or evidence, and marked when the storm had moved it. The agents read only sources whose terms allowed it, and refused or held the rest. They held a public key for their captures of event pages, because those pages showed guests' names. Every run was traced into Elastic, the work became a graph in Neo4j, and anyone could query the whole guide in SQL in their own browser. Part nine of the series.

item.title: From a feed to meaning: what the Storm Charles site did with public data that our new data site does not do yet, finding a source, reading its terms, writing parsers, keeping provenance, drawing it and saying what it means, three source sites to show it hourly, for the weather, the sea and fire risk, and the relay of briefs from this newsroom to the agents that will build them
item.description: Comparing the Storm Charles site with our new data site, data.promptugal.news, shows the difference between collecting data and understanding it. In a night, the storm site found its sources, read their terms, wrote parsers and converters, kept every value with its source and time, labelled each line fact, evidence or hypothesis, drew it a dozen ways, the lead time from warning to decision, warned against observed, a replay, and then said what it meant. The data site, built yesterday from my brief, does the first half very well: nine public sources, IPMA's warnings, observations, forecasts, fire risk, sea and UV, MeteoAlarm and flights around Faro, collected by code, served as JSON with an API and an OpenAPI description, each value with its provenance. It does not yet draw it, explain it, or show anyone how to use it; and when I checked this morning, the "hourly" data had last been read at 02:28, six hours earlier. So here is the next step: three source sites, website cells each built on one feed that changes through the day, the weather and its warnings, the sea, and fire risk, each rebuilt every hour, each with its charts, a plain "what changed", and a page on how to use the data. It is a working example of connecting any data with any data. And the way this brief travels is itself the example: from this newsroom, to PrompTugal's conductor, to the conductor on another account, to the agent that runs the data; and to the AgentiCCells team that will build the sites.

item.title: Start with an interview: how someone goes from "I want to try it" to editing their own site with Claude, by being interviewed by Claude first, about what they want, the sections, their materials and the sites they like, then sending their material in whichever way suits them, getting five designs inspired by what they like, or a better version of the site they already have, and reaching the one milestone that matters
item.description: When someone says "cool, I want to try it", what happens next decides whether they ever get a website. Today the first step on agenticcells.ai is an email with our questions in it. I think we can do something much better, and show the power of Claude at the same time: start with an interview. Claude interviews the person about what they want the site to do, the sections they would like, the materials and documents they have, and, the question I like most, which websites they like and why. The answers become the brief. The material can come in whatever way suits them: a zip, an email, links to what is already public, or their own encrypted vault; and the interviewing Claude can even be the one that starts building. The five designs are then inspired by the sites they chose, which is what already happens with our best ones. Someone with a site already can start from it instead, and get a better version back. And all of it is aimed at one milestone: the moment the person changes their own site by talking to Claude. That is when they have what we sell.

item.title: The pitch: a site that looks better, that you own, that nobody can lock you into, that has almost nothing to attack, that costs once instead of every month, and that you change by talking to Claude, six promises, the proof behind each, and three designs for a site built on nothing else, "six promises", "just say it" and "stop renting your website"
item.description: Writing about WordPress, Wix and Squarespace, one sentence came out that I think is the whole offer: a site that looks better, that you own, that nobody can lock you into, that has almost nothing to attack, that costs once instead of every month, and that you change by talking to Claude. So I took it seriously. It is six promises, and each one has a proof we can already show: five designs by a team of agents; a repository in your own name; static files that move to any host; no server code, database, plugins or cookies; £250 once, at the launch price, instead of a monthly bill; and Claude as the editor, with guard rails. Then I asked a designer agent to build three sites on the pitch alone, each telling it in a different order and voice. "Six promises" sets the sentence itself as the headline, for anyone. "Just say it" leads with a conversation, the owner handing Claude a CV and the site changing, for technologists and people who hate page builders. "Stop renting your website" leads with owning against renting, for people leaving a platform. All three show the sites we have already made, for Yiheng Wang, Silvio Switha and José Bota. My recommendation: "six promises" on the home page, and the other two as the pages we send to their audiences.

item.title: You bring the business, we build the site: the AgentiCCells partner programme as it now stands on agenticcells.ai, one page per kind of partner, each with four figures, the fit, the flow, who does what and the money, a launch price of £250 with free evaluations every day, partner terms published, five designs on every page and ten languages from day one, all built in a night by the site's own agent team from two newsroom articles
item.description: Last night I wrote the partner programme here, and handed it to the agent team that runs agenticcells.ai to build. By the morning it was there, better than I had written it. The site now has a tagline its team came up with, which I like a lot: "Partners: you bring the business, we build the site". It has one page per kind of partner, the freelancer, the consultancy and the firm, each standing alone so I can send one link to one person, and each with four figures: how the parts fit together, how a deal runs in six steps, who does what across four lanes, and the money, 50/50 of the sale with hosting, support and retainers kept entirely by the partner. The launch price is £250, against an anchor of £500, and every day we build a limited number of sites free, for evaluation, for anyone who applies. The partner terms are published as terms, not a draft. Every page has five designs, and the whole site is in ten languages, Portuguese, French and Spanish in two variants each, German, Chinese and Japanese, because a partner programme should be international from the first day. Nothing has been sold and no partner has signed yet; this week I start sending the links.

item.title: Static against the platforms: why a static site in your own repository, edited by Claude and watched by a security agent, is a real alternative to WordPress, Wix and Squarespace, what the numbers say about their reach, their attack surface, their complexity and their lock-in, and a converter that could bring a WordPress or Squarespace site across
item.description: I think the website cell has a real market, and the place to look for it is the people already running a site on WordPress, Wix or Squarespace. Those platforms are not short of features; they are full of them, and full of complexity. I know people who maintain WordPress sites, and I remember one where changing a banner did not work, and nobody could update it normally. The numbers back that up. WordPress runs 38.5% of all websites; Wix has 6.1 million paying subscriptions; Squarespace had more than 5.2 million when it last said. In 2025, 11,334 new vulnerabilities were found in the WordPress ecosystem, 91% of them in plugins, 46% with no fix when they were disclosed, and the worst ones were mass-exploited a median of five hours after. A third of WordPress sites run an older major version; 60% use a page builder; only 45% pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Wix's sites cannot be moved off Wix, and Squarespace exports only part of a site; both raised prices this year. Against that, a website cell is static: no server code, no database, no plugins to patch, no cookies unless the owner adds them, served as files. Its editor is Claude, which can do far more than any page editor; and it ships with a security agent that checks what the owner's changes expose. The owner can still shoot themselves in the foot, and that is a service a partner can sell. And because WordPress exports everything, and Squarespace exports in WordPress's format, one converter could bring a large share of those sites across.

item.title: Partners sell, we build: the AgentiCCells partner programme in full, three kinds of partner, a freelancer, a small consultancy and a larger firm, what each one sells, the agent team behind even the smallest website cell, the rules of engagement, who owns what, who invoices, who gets paid and when, what stays with the partner, and why a partner who takes the open code and does it alone is still a win
item.description: Our go-to-market for the website cell is not to compete with the people who already sell websites, workflows and IT to small businesses. It is to give them what we have. This is the partner programme, written so I can send it to the people I already have in mind this week. There are three kinds of partner: a freelancer who talks to people and wants to sell more; a small consultancy with customers who want this; and a larger firm with bigger projects, which wants us, or my network of experts, involved. What they sell is the unit we now make: a website cell, a GitHub repository fully set up with a live site, a CLAUDE.md and a behaviour policy, five designs by a team of agents, and the site handed over to its owner's Claude. Even the smallest one is a team of agents, a conductor, a designer, a developer, a researcher and a security reviewer, each with a job description, and that team is what partners resell. The rules are simple. If I am involved, doing the orchestration and running the factory, the sale is split 50/50. Whoever brings the customer invoices them. The customer owns the site. Hosting, support and monthly retainers belong to the partner, entirely: I do not do subscriptions. My part is the set-up, and then new features, templates, workflows and behaviour policies. It works in any country and any language. And a partner who reads this, takes the open source and does it alone, is still a win: one more team running our technology, and one more place agent behaviour policies are used for real.

item.title: The website cell: what we now sell, a GitHub repository fully set up with a live site on its own address, a CLAUDE.md and a behaviour policy, five designs by a team of agents, and then the site is yours to change with your own Claude, what it should cost, how it compares with Wix, Squarespace, Framer, Lovable and a freelancer, who already sells something close to it, and where to find buyers and partners
item.description: Everyone I show our sites to asks for one. So this is the offer, mapped. A website cell is one unit: a GitHub repository fully configured, with a live site on GitHub Pages at its own address, HTTPS, CI checks, a CLAUDE.md written for its owner and an agent behaviour policy, all set up automatically by our site factory. Then a team of agents, a designer, a developer and the rest, works from the person's photos, videos and words and makes five designs to choose from, the way we did for Yiheng Wang, Silvio Switha and Gabriel. Then it is handed over, and the person changes it with their own Claude: Yiheng gave Claude her CV as a PDF, and it read it and added her latest experience to the site. That combination, a site that looks professional, five designs, and full control by its owner with guard rails, is to me the best embodiment of what Claude can do now. The anchor price is £500, one-off, with a launch price still to decide. Against it: AI builders at £9 to £30 a month that lock the site in; vibe-coding tools at £20 to £30 a month plus credits; a freelancer at £800 to £3,000 for a small site. Nobody else hands over a repository with its own agent rules. And the real reason I want to sell many: every website cell is an agent behaviour policy working in the world.
